etymology: From “trump” (a trumpet), through Old French trompe; the final trumpet-blast of God at the resurrection and return of Christ.
biblical_def: The last trump is the final trumpet-blast that shall sound at the coming of Christ, summoning the dead to rise and the living to be changed. The apostle reveals the mystery: “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” Paul tells the Thessalonians that the Lord Himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God, and the dead in Christ shall rise first. Our Lord foretold that He shall send His angels with a great sound of a trumpet to gather His elect from the four winds. The trumpet runs back through Scripture as the signal of God's presence and summons—at Sinai, in the jubilee, in the assembling of Israel—and here it is the signal of the consummation. The dictionary holds the last trump to teach the bodily resurrection and the instantaneous transformation of the living saints at one and the same moment, the return of Christ. It is “last” as the final summons of history, not the eighth of a series of secret raptures. The dictionary therefore marks it against the dispensational scheme that divides the coming of Christ into separate stages—a secret rapture before a tribulation and a later public appearing—for Scripture sets the resurrection of the dead, the changing of the living, and the gathering of the elect at one trumpet, the last. The doctrine is the comfort of the bereaved and the hope of the church: at the last trump the graves shall yield their dead, mortality shall put on immortality, and death shall be swallowed up in victory.
webster_summary: The final trumpet-blast at the coming of Christ, when the dead are raised incorruptible and the living changed in a moment (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16); “last” as history's final summons, against a staged secret rapture.
webster_full: LAST TRUMP, noun phrase. [Old French trompe, a trumpet.] The final trumpet-blast at the return of Christ.
“At the last trump… the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52).
The Lord descends with the trump of God, and the dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16).
Christ sends His angels with a great sound of a trumpet to gather the elect (Matthew 24:31).
“Last” as history's final summons, not one of a staged series of comings.
scriptures: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.
Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
corruption_summary: Dispensationalism divides the coming of Christ into a secret rapture and a later public appearing, against the single “last trump” that raises the dead and changes the living at one moment.
corruption_paragraphs: The dispensational scheme, a nineteenth-century novelty associated with Darby and Scofield, divides the second coming into two events separated by a seven-year tribulation: a secret rapture of the church, then a later public return. The dictionary rejects this on the plain testimony of the texts. Paul places the resurrection of the dead and the changing of the living at the last trump—a single, final, audible summons; the Lord descends with a shout and the trump of God, hardly a secret event; and the gathering of the elect is joined to the trumpet's great sound. To carve a hidden rapture out of these passages and postpone the public appearing is to read into Scripture a scheme it nowhere teaches.

The recovery is the unity and finality of the consummation. The last trump sounds once, and at its sounding the whole work is done: the dead in Christ rise, the living saints are transformed, the elect are gathered, and the Lord is openly revealed. The dictionary holds this against the speculative timetables and prophecy-charts that have led many astray, and rests the church's hope where the apostle rests it—not in escaping tribulation by a secret removal, but in the sure and public coming of Christ, when mortality shall put on immortality and death be swallowed up in victory. This hope the apostle commends as comfort: wherefore comfort one another with these words.
roots_summary: From the Greek salpinx (trumpet) and eschate salpinx (“the last trumpet”); the trumpet is the recurring biblical signal of God's presence, summons, and the consummation.
roots_lines: Salpinx, Greek, a trumpet, the instrument of God's summons.
Eschate salpinx, “the last trumpet,” the final blast of 1 Corinthians 15:52.
Shophar, the Hebrew ram's-horn trumpet of Sinai and the jubilee.
“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” (Greek en atomo) marks the change as instantaneous.
The “shout” (Greek keleusma) and “voice of the archangel” show the coming to be public, not secret.
usage: The pastor comforted the bereaved with the last trump, when the dead in Christ shall rise incorruptible.
He showed that one trumpet raises the dead and changes the living, against the two-stage dispensational coming.

etymology: From Babylon, the ancient city of pride and idolatry, taken up in the Revelation as the symbolic name of the great harlot-city opposed to God and His people.
biblical_def: Babylon the Great is the symbolic name given in the Revelation to the great harlot-city that embodies the world-system in its pride, idolatry, luxury, and hatred of the people of God. Upon her forehead is written, “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.” She sits upon many waters and upon a beast; she is drunken with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus; she is the seat of the world's commerce, seduction, and false worship. Her doom is certain: an angel cries mightily, “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen,” and a voice from heaven summons God's people, “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.” The dictionary follows the historic Protestant and Reformed reading that sees in Babylon, beyond the literal ancient city, the great enemy-system of every age—the world in its organized rebellion against God—and, in the Reformers' particular application, the corrupt and persecuting power of false religion seated in a great city. Interpreters differ over the precise referent (apostate Rome, the persecuting world-empire, the final manifestation of antichristian power), and the dictionary does not bind the conscience to a single identification. What is certain is the moral meaning: Babylon is the city of man set against the city of God, glorious and seductive in her luxuries, bloody in her persecutions, and appointed to fall. The summons to the saints is the abiding application: come out of her, be not partakers of her sins, set your hope on the city that hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
webster_summary: The symbolic harlot-city of Revelation 17-18 embodying the world-system in pride, idolatry, luxury, and persecution; drunken with the blood of the saints and appointed to fall, with the summons, “Come out of her, my people.”

“MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS” (Revelation 17:5).
Drunken with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus (Revelation 17:6).

The summons: “Come out of her, my people” (Revelation 18:4).

corruption_summary: The sensational date-setting school turns Babylon into a coded prediction of current events and headlines, while the spiritualizing school empties her of all reference to real, judgable evil.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption, found in much popular prophecy teaching, reduces Babylon the Great to a cipher for the latest headline—a particular nation, a coming world government, a rebuilt city—and reads the Revelation as a coded almanac of current events. The dictionary counsels sobriety. The Spirit gave Babylon as a moral and theological symbol of the world-system in its pride, idolatry, and persecution; she has worn many faces through history, and interpreters may reasonably differ on her precise referent without making the text a newspaper to be decoded afresh each decade.

The opposite corruption spiritualizes Babylon into a vague principle with no real referent and no real judgment, so that the summons “come out of her” loses its edge. But Babylon is no abstraction: she is drunken with the blood of the martyrs, and her fall is the vindication of the saints she slew. The dictionary holds the historic Protestant reading that sees in her the organized worldly and false-religious power opposed to Christ, and presses the abiding application: God's people are summoned to separate from her sins, to refuse her luxuries and her idolatries, and to set their hope on the city of God that shall stand when Babylon is fallen.
roots_summary: From Babylon (Hebrew Babel, “confusion”), the ancient city of pride and idolatry, taken into the Revelation as the type of the world-system; “mystery” (Greek mysterion) marks the name as symbolic.
roots_lines: Babel, Hebrew, “confusion,” the city of the tower and the type of human pride against God.
Mysterion, Greek, “mystery,” marking “Babylon” here as a symbolic name.
Porne, Greek, harlot, the figure of the seductive, idolatrous world-city.
“Drunken with the blood of the saints” names her as the persecutor of the church.
“Come out of her” echoes the call to flee literal Babylon (Jeremiah 51:45).
usage: The pastor preached Babylon the Great as the world-system in its pride and persecution, summoning the saints to come out of her.
He warned against decoding Babylon as the day's headlines, reading her instead as the Spirit gave her.
She set her hope on the city of God, refusing the luxuries and idolatries of fallen Babylon.

etymology: From the Revelation's vision of the consummated union of Christ and His church under the figure of a wedding feast; the Lamb the Bridegroom, the church His bride.
biblical_def: The marriage supper of the Lamb is the Revelation's figure for the consummated, eternal union of Christ and His church, celebrated as a wedding feast at the end of the age. The voice of heaven cries, “Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready,” and the angel declares, “Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.” The bride is the new Jerusalem, the church glorified, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The figure gathers up a long biblical theme: the LORD as the husband of His people, the prophets' promise of betrothal, the Lord's own parables of the wedding and the bridegroom, and the apostle's teaching that Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, that He might present it to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle, holy and without blemish. The dictionary holds the marriage supper to teach the goal of redemption: not merely the rescue of sinners from wrath but their everlasting fellowship and joy with Christ in the closest and most blessed of unions. It is the answer to the longing of the bride and the reward of the Bridegroom's love. The dictionary marks the figure against the carnal misreadings that would literalize or sensualize it, and against the gloom that conceives of heaven as bare survival; the consummation is a feast, a wedding, the fulness of joy in the presence of the Lamb, where the redeemed shall behold His face and be His for ever.
webster_summary: The Revelation's figure for the consummated, eternal union of Christ and His church as a wedding feast (Revelation 19:7-9); the Lamb the Bridegroom, the new Jerusalem His bride made ready—the goal and joy of redemption.
webster_full: MARRIAGE SUPPER OF THE LAMB, noun phrase. The wedding feast figuring the eternal union of Christ and His church.
“The marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).
“Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).
The bride is the new Jerusalem, adorned for her husband (Revelation 21:2).
Christ presents the church to Himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27).

And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God.

Eph 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the carnal literalizing or sensualizing of the figure, and the gloomy reduction of heaven to bare survival rather than the fulness of joy with Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the relational and joyful goal of redemption. Some err by literalizing or sensualizing the marriage figure, as though heaven were carnal pleasure; the Lord Himself taught that in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. The wedding of the Lamb is the figure of the most intimate and blessed union, the church's everlasting fellowship and joy with Christ, not a sensual reward. The dictionary reads the symbol as the Spirit gave it: the consummation of covenant love between the Bridegroom and His bride.

The opposite corruption conceives of heaven as bare survival or endless solemnity, a pale and joyless existence. The marriage supper rebukes this gloom. The consummation is a feast and a wedding, attended by gladness and rejoicing and the giving of honour to the Lamb; the bride, washed and adorned, enters the fulness of joy in her Husband's presence. The dictionary holds that redemption's end is not merely escape from wrath but the everlasting delight of the redeemed in Christ, who will present them to Himself a glorious church and dwell with them, their God, and wipe away all tears from their eyes.
roots_summary: From the Greek gamos tou arniou (“marriage of the Lamb”) and deipnon (supper, the chief evening meal); the Lamb (arnion) is the slain and risen Bridegroom.
roots_lines: Gamos, Greek, a marriage or wedding feast.
Deipnon, Greek, the chief meal, here the festal supper of the consummation.
Arnion, Greek, the Lamb, the slain and risen Christ as Bridegroom.
Nymphe, Greek, the bride, the new Jerusalem, the glorified church.
The Old Testament marriage-figure of the LORD and His people is fulfilled in the Lamb and His church.
usage: The pastor preached the marriage supper of the Lamb as the joyful goal of redemption, the bride forever with her Husband.
He set the wedding feast against the gloomy notion of heaven as bare survival.
She longed for the day when the bride, made ready, should enter the fulness of joy with the Lamb.

etymology: The second chapter of the Revelation of Jesus Christ, containing the first four of the seven letters to the churches of Asia—Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, and Thyatira.
biblical_def: Revelation 2 is the chapter containing the first four of the seven letters which the risen Christ, walking among the golden candlesticks, dictated to John for the churches of Asia—Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, and Thyatira. Each letter follows a pattern: a title of Christ drawn from the opening vision, a commendation of what is praiseworthy, a rebuke of what is amiss, a call to repent or endure, and a promise to him that overcometh. To Ephesus, busy and orthodox, the Lord says, “I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love,” calling her to remember, repent, and do the first works, lest He remove her candlestick. To Smyrna, poor and persecuted, He gives no rebuke but only comfort: “Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.” To Pergamos, dwelling where Satan's seat is, He warns against the doctrine of Balaam and the Nicolaitanes. To Thyatira He commends growing love and service but condemns the toleration of Jezebel, the false prophetess seducing His servants. The dictionary holds Revelation 2 to teach the searching, particular knowledge of Christ over His churches: He walks among them, knows their works, commends, rebukes, and warns. The letters are not merely ancient correspondence but a perpetual mirror for the church of every age—against the loss of first love, the toleration of false teaching, the fear of suffering, and compromise with the world. To each the same refrain sounds: “He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.”
webster_summary: The chapter containing the first four letters of the risen Christ to the churches—Ephesus (left first love), Smyrna (faithful unto death), Pergamos (Satan's seat), Thyatira (toleration of Jezebel); a perpetual mirror for the church of every age.
webster_full: REVELATION 2, proper noun. The second chapter of the Revelation, with four of the seven letters to the churches.
To Ephesus: “Thou hast left thy first love” (Revelation 2:4); remember, repent, do the first works.
To Smyrna: “Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Revelation 2:10).
To Pergamos and Thyatira: warnings against false doctrine and the toleration of Jezebel.
Each closes: “He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.”

Re 2:5

Re 2:7

corruption_summary: The dispensational scheme turns the seven churches into a coded timeline of church-age periods, while the critical school empties the letters of their abiding address to the church of every age.
corruption_paragraphs: A popular dispensational reading treats the seven churches as a prophetic outline of seven successive ages of church history, so that Ephesus is the apostolic age, Laodicea the apostate last age, and the others ranged between. The dictionary regards this as a speculative imposition. The letters were written to seven real churches of Asia, addressing their actual condition, and they speak to every church in every age by the perpetual relevance of their warnings and promises—not by a hidden chronological code. To read them as a timeline is to obscure their plain pastoral purpose.

The opposite error, found in some critical scholarship, treats the letters as merely first-century occasional correspondence with no abiding claim on the church today. But the risen Christ who walks among the candlesticks still knows the works of His churches, and the refrain “he that hath an ear, let him hear” addresses all the churches in every age. The dictionary holds Revelation 2 as a living word: a mirror in which the church of every generation may see her loss of first love, her temptation to fear suffering, her flirtation with false doctrine and worldly compromise, and may hear afresh the call to repent, endure, and overcome.
roots_summary: From the seven letters dictated by the risen Christ; the “candlestick” (Greek luchnia) figures each church, and “him that overcometh” (ho nikon) names the persevering believer.
roots_lines: Luchnia, Greek, a lampstand or candlestick, the figure of each church (Revelation 1:20).
Ho nikon, Greek, “he that overcometh,” the persevering believer to whom promises are made.
“First love” (Greek ten agapen sou ten proten) names Ephesus's loss.
“Faithful unto death” (Greek pistos achri thanatou) is the charge to Smyrna.
The pattern—title, commendation, rebuke, call, promise—structures each letter.
usage: The pastor preached Revelation 2 to call a busy, orthodox church back from the loss of its first love.
He comforted the suffering with the word to Smyrna, to be faithful unto death for the crown of life.
She read the letters as a mirror for her own church, not a coded timeline of the ages.

pos: noun phrase (the symbolic numbers of Revelation)
etymology: From “apocalyptic” (Greek apokalypsis, an unveiling) and “measurements”; the symbolic dimensions and numbers given in the Revelation, as the measuring of the city and temple.
biblical_def: Apocalyptic measurements are the symbolic dimensions and numbers given in the Revelation—the measuring of the temple, the city foursquare of twelve thousand furlongs, the wall of a hundred forty and four cubits—which convey spiritual truth through significant figures rather than mere surveyor's data. An angel with a golden reed measures the new Jerusalem, and the city lieth foursquare, its length, breadth, and height equal: a perfect cube, recalling the holy of holies, the dwelling of God now enlarging to embrace all His people. The wall is a hundred forty and four cubits, twelve times twelve, the number of the tribes and the apostles multiplied—the fulness of the covenant people. John is given a reed to measure the temple of God and them that worship therein, a sign of God's preservation and ownership of His true worshippers. The dictionary holds that these measurements are to be read as the apocalyptic genre intends: numerically symbolic, freighted with meaning—twelve for the covenant people, the cube for the divine presence, perfect dimensions for the perfected church—not as literal architectural specifications for a future structure. The act of measuring itself signifies divine ownership, protection, and the certainty of God's purpose. The dictionary marks this against two errors: the wooden literalism that turns the figures into blueprints for a rebuilt temple or a calculable city, missing the symbolism the genre demands; and the dismissive spiritualism that empties the numbers of any real meaning. Read aright, the apocalyptic measurements declare that God knows, owns, protects, and perfects His people, and that the city He builds for them is laid out by His own hand in the perfect proportions of His presence.
webster_summary: The symbolic dimensions and numbers of the Revelation—the foursquare city of twelve thousand furlongs, the wall of 144 cubits, the measuring of the temple—conveying spiritual truth through significant figures, not literal blueprints.
webster_full: APOCALYPTIC MEASUREMENTS, noun phrase. The symbolic dimensions and numbers of the Revelation.
The city lieth foursquare, twelve thousand furlongs, length, breadth, and height equal (Revelation 21:16).
The wall is a hundred forty and four cubits—twelve times twelve (Revelation 21:17).
John is given a reed to measure the temple and them that worship therein (Revelation 11:1).
Numerically symbolic—the cube of God's presence, the twelve of His people—not literal blueprints.

And he measured the wall thereof, an hundred and forty and four cubits, according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel.

corruption_summary: Wooden literalism turns the figures into blueprints for a rebuilt temple or a calculable city, while dismissive spiritualism empties the numbers of all meaning; both miss the symbolism the apocalyptic genre demands.
corruption_paragraphs: The literalist error, common in dispensational prophecy teaching, treats the apocalyptic measurements as architectural specifications—calculating the cubits of a future temple or the miles of a literal cubic city floating above the earth. The dictionary regards this as a misreading of the genre. Apocalyptic literature speaks in significant numbers and figures: twelve for the covenant people, a hundred forty-four for their fulness, the cube for the holy of holies where God dwells. To reduce these to a builder's plan is to trade the rich symbolism the Spirit intended for a wooden literalism the text does not bear.

The opposite error so spiritualizes the figures that they mean nothing definite at all, a vague gesture toward heaven with no content. But the numbers are precise and purposeful: the perfect cube declares that the whole city is now the dwelling-place of God, the twelves declare it the home of the covenant people, and the act of measuring declares God's ownership and protection of His own. The dictionary holds the apocalyptic measurements as genuine revelation in symbolic dress—teaching that God knows, owns, guards, and perfects His people, and builds for them a city of perfect proportions, the eternal dwelling of His presence.
roots_summary: From apokalypsis (an unveiling) and the measuring imagery of the Revelation; the “reed” (Greek kalamos) and the numbers twelve and its multiples carry the symbolism.
roots_lines: Apokalypsis, Greek, an unveiling or revelation, the genre of symbolic vision.
Kalamos, Greek, a reed or measuring-rod, the angel's instrument.
Twelve and its multiples (144; 12,000) signify the fulness of the covenant people.
The “foursquare” cube recalls the holy of holies, the dwelling of God.
The act of measuring signifies divine ownership, protection, and sure purpose.
usage: The teacher read the foursquare city as the symbol of God's dwelling enlarged to His whole people, not a literal cube.
He warned against turning the apocalyptic measurements into blueprints for a rebuilt temple.
She saw in the measuring of the temple the LORD's ownership and protection of His true worshippers.

etymology: Plural of the Greek stadion, a unit of length of about 600 feet (an eighth of a Roman mile), rendered “furlong” in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: A stadion (plural stadia) is the Greek unit of distance, about six hundred feet or an eighth of a Roman mile, rendered “furlong” in the Authorized Version. It appears in the New Testament to mark real distances and, in the Revelation, to convey symbolic measure. Luke records that Emmaus was about threescore furlongs from Jerusalem; John that the disciples had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs when they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and that Bethany was about fifteen furlongs off. In the Revelation the unit carries symbolic weight: the blood from the winepress of God's wrath flowed by the space of a thousand and six hundred furlongs, and the holy city measured twelve thousand furlongs every way. The dictionary notes the term chiefly to aid the plain reading of Scripture: the furlongs of the Gospels are honest measurements that ground the narratives in real geography—the resurrection appearances, the storm on Galilee, the road to Bethany—and so witness against the notion that the Gospel events float free of time and place. The figures of the Revelation, by contrast, belong to the symbolic register of apocalyptic and are read for their significance (sixteen hundred as four squared times a hundred, a measure of completeness in judgment; twelve thousand as the fulness of the covenant city). The dictionary holds the sound principle of interpretation: a measurement in a historical narrative is a real distance, while a measurement in an apocalyptic vision is a significant symbol, and the genre of the passage determines how the figure is to be read.
webster_summary: The Greek unit of distance (about 600 feet, an eighth of a Roman mile), rendered “furlong” in the AV; a real measure grounding the Gospel narratives in geography, and a symbolic measure in the visions of the Revelation.
webster_full: STADIA, noun. [Plural of Greek stadion.] A unit of distance of about 600 feet, the AV “furlong.”
Emmaus was about threescore furlongs from Jerusalem (Luke 24:13).
The disciples rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs on Galilee (John 6:19).
Bethany was about fifteen furlongs off (John 11:18).
In the Revelation it carries symbolic measure (the city of 12,000 furlongs).
scriptures: And, behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was from Jerusalem about threescore furlongs.
Joh 6:19
So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs, they see Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing nigh unto the ship: and they were afraid.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the loss of the principle that a measure in narrative is literal geography while a measure in apocalyptic vision is symbolic.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is sound, genre-sensitive interpretation. The furlongs of the Gospels are honest distances—Emmaus threescore furlongs off, the rowing of the disciples, the nearness of Bethany—and they ground the sacred narrative in real and verifiable geography, witnessing against the critical notion that the Gospel events are timeless myth detached from place. The evangelists wrote of things that happened in measurable space, and the furlong-marks are a quiet evidence of their historical character.

Yet the same unit, set in the apocalyptic visions of the Revelation, belongs to a symbolic register: a thousand six hundred furlongs of blood, twelve thousand furlongs of the holy city. To read these as land-survey is as mistaken as to read the Emmaus furlongs as mystical numbers. The dictionary holds the abiding rule of interpretation: the genre of a passage governs how its figures are read; measurements in historical narrative are literal, measurements in apocalyptic vision are significant symbols, and to confuse the two is to err either by mythologizing history or by literalizing symbol.
roots_summary: From the Greek stadion, a measure of about 600 feet and the name of the racecourse of that length (whence “stadium”); the AV renders it by the English “furlong.”
roots_lines: Stadion, Greek, a unit of about 600 feet, an eighth of a Roman mile.
The same word names the racecourse of that length, the root of “stadium.”
“Furlong,” the AV rendering, an English measure of 220 yards.
In narrative, a literal distance grounding the events in geography.
In apocalyptic vision, a symbolic measure freighted with significance.

She read the twelve thousand furlongs of the city as the fulness of God's people, not a survey.

etymology: From the visions of Daniel; the four successive world-empires figured by the parts of the great image and by the four beasts, before the everlasting kingdom of God.
biblical_def: The four kingdoms are the succession of world-empires revealed to Daniel, twice over: in Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the great image with its head of gold, breast of silver, belly of brass, and legs of iron; and in Daniel's vision of four great beasts rising from the sea. The angel interprets the beasts plainly: “These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth.” Daniel is told he himself, in Babylon, is the head of gold, and that after him three more kingdoms should arise. The historic and Reformed identification reads the four as Babylon (gold), Medo-Persia (silver), Greece (brass), and Rome (iron)—the empires that bestrode the world from Daniel's day to the coming of Christ. The point of both visions is not the empires themselves but their end: in the days of those last kings the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, a stone cut without hands that smote the image and became a great mountain filling the earth. The kingdom and dominion shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High, whose kingdom is everlasting. The dictionary holds the four kingdoms to teach the sovereignty of God over the rise and fall of nations and the certainty of the everlasting kingdom of Christ, established at His first coming and to be consummated at His last. The dictionary marks this against the dispensational reading that severs the iron kingdom from history to make it a revived future empire, and against the rationalist late-dating of Daniel that denies its predictive prophecy; the visions are genuine prophecy, given before the events, displaying the God who changeth the times and seasons and removeth and setteth up kings.
webster_summary: The four successive world-empires of Daniel's visions—the great image and the four beasts—historically Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome, before the everlasting kingdom of God set up by the stone cut without hands (Daniel 2:44).
webster_full: FOUR KINGDOMS, noun phrase. The four world-empires of Daniel's visions, figured by the image and the four beasts.
“These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth” (Daniel 7:17).
Historically read as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome.
In their days God sets up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44).
The dominion is given to the saints of the most High, an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:27).
scriptures: And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.
These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth.
And wheresoever the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven hath he given into thine hand, and hath made thee ruler over them all. Thou art this head of gold.

And the kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven, shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
corruption_summary: Dispensationalism severs the iron kingdom from history to make it a revived future empire, while rationalist late-dating denies Daniel any genuine predictive prophecy.
corruption_paragraphs: The dispensational reading severs the fourth kingdom (the iron, historically Rome) from its historical fulfilment and projects it forward as a revived Roman empire of the end times, inserting a vast gap between the ancient empire and a future antichristian confederacy. The dictionary regards this as a speculative imposition driven by the dispensational system rather than the text. The stone smote the image in the days of the four kingdoms—at the first coming of Christ, when the everlasting kingdom of God was set up—not in a postponed future after a parenthesis of church-age centuries Daniel never foresaw.

The opposite corruption is the rationalist late-dating of Daniel, which assigns the book to the second century B.C., after the events it “predicts,” so as to deny it any genuine predictive prophecy. The dictionary rejects this on the authority of the Lord Jesus, who spoke of “Daniel the prophet,” and on the internal claims of the book itself. Daniel prophesied true things before they came to pass, displaying the God who changeth the times and the seasons, who removeth kings and setteth up kings. The four kingdoms teach the sovereignty of God over the nations and the triumph of the kingdom of Christ, established at His first coming and to be consummated at His return.
roots_summary: From the Aramaic visions of Daniel: the tselem (image) of four metals and the four cheyvan (beasts); the “stone cut without hands” figures the kingdom of God.
roots_lines: Tselem, Aramaic, the image of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, in four descending metals.
Cheyvan, Aramaic, the beasts of Daniel's vision, “four kings… out of the earth.”
Gold, silver, brass, and iron mark the four successive empires.
The “stone cut without hands” (Daniel 2:34) figures the kingdom of God, not raised by man.
The everlasting kingdom “which shall never be destroyed” is the kingdom of Christ and His saints.
usage: The teacher read the four kingdoms as Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome, with the stone striking in the days of Rome.
He defended Daniel as genuine predictive prophecy against the rationalist late-dating.
She took comfort that the God who sets up and casts down kingdoms has established the kingdom that cannot fall.

etymology: From the Lord's parable of the merchant seeking goodly pearls; the one pearl of supreme worth for which a man sells all that he has.
biblical_def: The pearl of great price is the figure of our Lord's brief parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.” It is twinned with the parable of the treasure hid in a field, which a man, having found, sold all that he had for joy to buy the field. Both parables teach the surpassing worth of the kingdom of heaven—of Christ and the salvation He gives—and the wholehearted forsaking of all else to gain it. The merchant does not stumble upon the pearl as the man stumbled on the treasure; he is a seeker, and finding the one pearl that outvalues all his stock, he gladly parts with everything to possess it. The dictionary reads the pearl as Christ Himself and His kingdom, before whose worth all earthly possessions, ambitions, and pleasures are rightly counted loss, as the apostle counted all things but dung that he might win Christ. The selling of all is not the purchase-price of merit—salvation is free, and the pearl is worth infinitely more than the all that is given—but the figure of a heart so gripped by the supreme value of Christ that it gladly lets everything else go. The dictionary marks the parable against the cheap discipleship that wants the pearl without the selling, clutching its earthly all while professing to value Christ; and against the works-righteousness that makes the selling a price that buys heaven. Rightly understood, the pearl of great price is the joy-driven renunciation of all for the One who is worth more than all.
webster_summary: The Lord's figure of the one pearl of supreme worth for which the merchant sells all that he has (Matthew 13:46); the surpassing value of Christ and His kingdom, and the joyful forsaking of all to gain Him.
webster_full: PEARL OF GREAT PRICE, noun phrase. The one pearl of supreme worth in the Lord's parable, for which a man sells all.
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls” (Matthew 13:45).
Finding one pearl of great price, he sold all that he had and bought it (Matthew 13:46).
Twinned with the treasure hid in a field, sold-all-for joyfully (Matthew 13:44).
The pearl is Christ and His kingdom, worth more than all that is given for it.
scriptures: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.
Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
corruption_summary: Cheap discipleship wants the pearl without the selling, clutching its earthly all; works-righteousness makes the selling a price that buys heaven—both miss the joyful renunciation of all for the One worth all.
corruption_paragraphs: Cheap discipleship hears the parable's offer—the pearl of great price—and ignores its cost, wanting Christ without forsaking anything, clutching its earthly possessions, ambitions, and sins while professing to value the kingdom. But the merchant sold all that he had. The dictionary names the error: a heart truly gripped by the surpassing worth of Christ will gladly let go what rivals Him, as the apostle counted all things loss to win Christ. To want the pearl without the selling is to prove one has not seen its worth.

The opposite error makes the selling a meritorious price that purchases heaven, as though the renunciation earned the pearl. But the pearl is worth infinitely more than the all that is given for it; the man does not pay its true value but gladly trades his lesser goods for the one supreme good. Salvation is free; the selling is not its purchase-price but the joyful response of a heart that has found the treasure. The dictionary holds the balance: the pearl of great price is freely given to faith, and the faith that receives it is a faith that, for joy, lets go of everything else to embrace the One who is worth more than all the world.
roots_summary: From the Greek margarites (pearl) and the parable's polytimos (of great price); the merchant (emporos) seeks goodly pearls and finds the one of supreme worth.
roots_lines: Margarites, Greek, a pearl, prized in the ancient world above gold.
Polytimos, Greek, “of great price,” of supreme value.
Emporos, Greek, a merchant, the seeker of goodly pearls.
“Sold all that he had” (Greek panta hosa eichen) marks the wholehearted renunciation.
Paul's “count all things but dung” (Philippians 3:8) is the parable lived out.
usage: The pastor preached the pearl of great price to show that Christ is worth more than all a man can give up for Him.
He warned against wanting the pearl without the selling, the cheap discipleship that forsakes nothing.
She counted her former gains but loss, having found the one pearl worth more than all the world.

etymology: From the Authorized Version's command to “be filled with the Spirit”; the believer's being controlled and empowered by the indwelling Holy Ghost.
biblical_def: The fulness of the Spirit is the believer's being filled, controlled, and empowered by the indwelling Holy Ghost, commanded by the apostle: “Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.” The command is in the continuous tense—be being filled—marking it not a once-for-all crisis but an ongoing condition the believer is to seek and walk in. The contrast with drunkenness is instructive: as wine fills and controls the drunkard, so the Spirit is to fill and govern the believer, but unto sobriety, holiness, and joy rather than excess. The fruit of being filled, the apostle goes on, is psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, thanksgiving, and mutual submission—a transformed life and worship. The book of Acts shows the apostles and the early church filled with the Holy Ghost for witness and boldness, speaking the word of God with power; and the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, longsuffering, and the rest—is the abiding mark of His fulness. The dictionary distinguishes the fulness of the Spirit from the indwelling of the Spirit, which every believer has from regeneration: all the saved are indwelt, but not all are filled, for filling is a matter of yielding to and being governed by the Spirit one already has. The dictionary marks the doctrine against two errors. The charismatic and Pentecostal teaching often makes the “baptism” or filling of the Spirit a second blessing evidenced by tongues, dividing Christians into two classes; but Scripture commands all believers to be filled and makes its evidence holiness and worship, not a sign-gift. The opposite error is the dead formalism that quenches the Spirit and walks in mere duty without His power. True fulness of the Spirit is the ordinary, commanded, Christ-exalting condition of the obedient believer, yielded to the Spirit who conforms him to Christ.
webster_summary: The believer's being filled, controlled, and empowered by the indwelling Holy Ghost (Ephesians 5:18); an ongoing condition commanded of all the saved, evidenced by holiness, worship, and the fruit of the Spirit, not by a sign-gift.
webster_full: FULNESS OF THE SPIRIT, noun phrase. The believer's being filled and governed by the indwelling Holy Ghost.
“Be not drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18), in the continuous tense.
Its fruit: psalms and spiritual songs, thanksgiving, holiness, and boldness in the word (Acts 4:31).
Distinct from the indwelling all believers have; filling is yielding to the Spirit one already has.
Evidenced by the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), not by a sign-gift.
scriptures: Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Ac 2:4
And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
corruption_summary: Pentecostal teaching often makes the filling a second blessing evidenced by tongues, dividing Christians into two classes; the opposite error is the dead formalism that quenches the Spirit and walks in mere duty.
corruption_paragraphs: Much Pentecostal and charismatic teaching turns the fulness of the Spirit into a distinct second blessing—a “baptism in the Spirit” subsequent to conversion and evidenced by speaking in tongues—thereby dividing believers into two classes, the merely converted and the Spirit-filled. The dictionary, holding to the cessationist Reformed position, rejects this scheme. Scripture commands all believers to be filled with the Spirit and names its evidence as holiness, thanksgiving, worship, and the fruit of the Spirit, not a sign-gift. Every Christian is indwelt by the Spirit from regeneration; the filling is the ongoing yielding to and empowering by the Spirit one already has, not the reception of a Spirit one lacked.

The opposite corruption is the dead formalism that has the form of godliness but denies its power, quenching and grieving the Spirit and walking in mere outward duty. Against this the apostle's command stands: be filled with the Spirit. The dictionary holds the balance: the fulness of the Spirit is neither a second-class elitism reserved for the few who claim a particular experience, nor a forgotten doctrine ceded to the formalist; it is the ordinary, commanded, Christ-exalting condition of every obedient believer, yielded to the indwelling Spirit who fills him unto holiness, joy, and conformity to Christ.
roots_summary: From the Greek plerousthe en Pneumati (“be filled with [or in] the Spirit”), a present-tense command of continual filling; distinct from the indwelling (oikeo) the Spirit has in every believer.
roots_lines: Plerousthe, Greek, “be filled,” a present continuous imperative—“be being filled.”
Pneuma, Greek, Spirit, the Holy Ghost who indwells and fills.
The contrast with being “drunk with wine” marks filling as control and governance.
Karpos tou Pneumatos, “the fruit of the Spirit” (Galatians 5:22), the evidence of His fulness.
Distinct from the Spirit's permanent indwelling of every believer from regeneration.
usage: The pastor preached the fulness of the Spirit as a command to all believers, evidenced by holiness and worship.
He answered the second-blessing teaching by showing that all the saved are indwelt and all are bidden to be filled.
She sought to be filled with the Spirit daily, yielding to the Comforter who conforms her to Christ.

etymology: From the Hebrew Chag Shavuot, “feast of weeks,” counted seven weeks (fifty days) from the firstfruits of barley; called Pentecost (Greek pentekoste, “fiftieth”) in the New Testament.
biblical_def: The feast of weeks is one of the three annual pilgrim-feasts of Israel, kept fifty days after the firstfruits of the barley harvest—seven weeks counted out—and so called in Greek Pentecost, the fiftieth day. It celebrated the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, when Israel brought a new meat offering and freewill gifts unto the LORD, rejoicing in His provision. “Thou shalt observe the feast of weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest”; and the people were to keep it with a tribute of a freewill offering, according as the LORD had blessed them. By the time of the New Testament it had also become associated with the giving of the law at Sinai, fifty days after the Passover-exodus. The dictionary marks the feast of weeks chiefly for its glorious fulfilment: it was when the day of Pentecost was fully come that the Holy Ghost descended upon the gathered church, and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost. As the feast brought the firstfruits of the harvest, so Pentecost brought the firstfruits of the gospel harvest, three thousand souls reaped in a day; and as the law was given at Sinai written on tables of stone, so at Pentecost the Spirit was given to write the law on the hearts of God's people. The dictionary holds the feast as a true type fulfilled in Christ and the Spirit: the old shadow of harvest and law gives way to the substance, the outpouring of the Spirit and the ingathering of the nations. To read it merely as an agricultural festival, severed from its fulfilment, is to miss the design of God, who appointed the feasts as shadows of things to come, the body of which is Christ.
webster_summary: One of Israel's three pilgrim-feasts, kept fifty days after the firstfruits of barley (Hebrew Shavuot; Greek Pentecost); the firstfruits of wheat harvest, fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit and the firstfruits of the gospel harvest (Acts 2:1).
webster_full: FEAST OF WEEKS, noun phrase. [Hebrew Chag Shavuot.] An annual feast of Israel, fifty days after the firstfruits of barley.
It celebrated the firstfruits of wheat harvest with a new meat offering (Exodus 34:22; Leviticus 23:16).
Kept with a freewill offering, according as the LORD had blessed (Deuteronomy 16:10).
Called Pentecost (“fiftieth”) in the New Testament, associated also with the giving of the law.
Fulfilled when the Spirit descended on the church at Pentecost (Acts 2:1).
scriptures: And thou shalt observe the feast of weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the year's end.

And thou shalt keep the feast of weeks unto the LORD thy God with a tribute of a freewill offering of thine hand, which thou shalt give unto the LORD thy God, according as the LORD thy God hath blessed thee:
Even unto the morrow after the seventh sabbath shall ye number fifty days; and ye shall offer a new meat offering unto the LORD.
Ac 2:1
And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is severing the feast from its fulfilment in Christ and the Spirit, reading it as a bare agricultural festival.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the typological fulfilment of the feasts in Christ. The critical habit reads the feast of weeks as merely an agricultural festival of the ancient Near East, a harvest celebration like those of the surrounding nations, severed from any redemptive meaning. The dictionary affirms the historical harvest setting but denies the severance: the apostle declares the feasts shadows of things to come, the body of which is Christ, and the descent of the Spirit on the day of Pentecost is the divinely appointed fulfilment of the feast of weeks.

Read in the line of Scripture, the feast is rich with design. As it brought the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, so Pentecost brought the firstfruits of the gospel harvest, three thousand souls in a day; as the law was given fifty days after the exodus at Sinai, so the Spirit was given fifty days after the Passover of Christ's death, to write the law on the heart. The dictionary holds the feast of weeks as a true type fulfilled: the shadow of harvest and law giving way to the substance, the outpouring of the Spirit and the gathering of the nations into the church of Christ.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew Shavuot (“weeks”), counted seven weeks from the firstfruits of barley; the Greek pentekoste (“fiftieth”) names the same day, Pentecost.
roots_lines: Chag Shavuot, Hebrew, “feast of weeks,” seven weeks after the barley firstfruits.
Pentekoste, Greek, “fiftieth” (day), the New Testament name Pentecost.
Bikkurim, Hebrew, firstfruits, the offering of the feast.
One of the three pilgrim-feasts (with Passover and Tabernacles) requiring appearance before the LORD.
Associated by tradition with the giving of the law at Sinai, fifty days after the exodus.
usage: The teacher showed how the feast of weeks was fulfilled when the Spirit fell at Pentecost.
He preached the firstfruits of wheat as a shadow of the firstfruits of the gospel harvest.
She read the feasts not as bare agriculture but as shadows whose body is Christ.
